g.text: SITUATIONAL RULE: competence × urgency picks the style
Novice + routine → DIRECT (teach, check); novice + emergency → AUTOCRATIC;
competent + change → DEMOCRATIC; expert + stable → LAISSEZ-FAIRE; broken
culture → TRANSFORMATIONAL. Servant leaders add: \"what do you need from me?\"
— removing obstacles so the team shines; the ward's success is their appraisal.
EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE (5 domains): self-awareness (know your triggers —
hunger, fatigue, disrespect), self-regulation (pause before reacting), motivation
(purpose beyond pay), empathy (feel the junior's first-night terror), social skill
(resolve, persuade, reconcile). High-EI in-charges get incident reports; low-EI
ones get cover-ups. Management = things (rosters, stock, budgets); leadership =
people (vision, trust, growth) — ward in-charges must do BOTH, switching by the
minute. Leading change: unfreeze (why now? data + story), move (pilot small,
support loudly), refreeze (protocol + audit + celebrate) — Lewin's 3 steps beat
"because I said so" every time. New graduates lead from day one: handovers,
students, relatives, emergencies — the uniform leads before the rank does.
Exam line: \"the best style is the one the SITUATION needs, not the leader prefers.\"
